The overall order is equal to sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the rate law.

The overall order of the reaction is 3.

questions.question: For a given chemical reaction {\gamma }_{1}A + {\gamma }_{2}B \to {\gamma }_{3}C + {\gamma }_{4}D$. Concentration of $C$ changes from $10\mathrm{mmol}{\mathrm{dm}}^{ - 3}$ to $20\mathrm{mmol}{\mathrm{dm}}^{ - 3}$ in $10s.$ Rate of appearance of $D$ is $1.5$ times the rate of disappearance of $B$ which is twice the rate of disappearance $A$. The rate of appearance of $D$ has been experimentally determined to be $9\mathrm{mmol}{\mathrm{dm}}^{ - 3}{s}^{ - 1}.$ Therefore the rate of reaction is____$\mathrm{mmol}{\mathrm{dm}}^{ - 3}{s}^{ - 1}.$ (Nearest Integer)

$\frac{d\left(c\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = \left(\frac{20 - 10}{10}\right) = 1\mathrm{milimole} / {\mathrm{dm}}^{3}\sec {\gamma }_{1}A + {\gamma }_{2}B \to {\gamma }_{3}C + {\gamma }_{4}D \frac{d\left(D\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = 1.5\left( - \frac{d}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(B\right)\right) = 9\mathrm{milimole} / {\mathrm{dm}}^{3}\sec \left( - \frac{d}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(B\right)\right) = 2\left( - \frac{d}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(A\right)\right)$

Rate $= - \frac{1}{{\gamma }_{1}}\frac{d\left(A\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = - \frac{1}{{\gamma }_{2}}\frac{d\left(B\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{1}{{\gamma }_{3}}\frac{d\left(C\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{1}{{\gamma }_{4}}\frac{d\left(D\right)}{\mathrm{dt}}$

(i) $\frac{d\left(D\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{{\gamma }_{4}}{{\gamma }_{2}}\left( - \frac{d\left(B\right)}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) = 1.5\left( - \frac{d}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(B\right)\right) \frac{{\gamma }_{4}}{{\gamma }_{2}} = 1.5$

(ii) $\frac{{\gamma }_{2}}{{\gamma }_{1}}\left( - \frac{d\left(A\right)}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) = \left( - \frac{d}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(B\right)\right) = 2\left( - \frac{d}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(A\right)\right) \frac{{\gamma }_{2}}{{\gamma }_{1}} = 2$

(iii) $\frac{d\left(C\right)}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{{\gamma }_{3}}{{\gamma }_{4}}\left(\frac{d\left(D\right)}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) 1 = \frac{{\gamma }_{3}}{{\gamma }_{4}} \times 9 \frac{{\gamma }_{4}}{{\gamma }_{3}} = 9$

So, if

{\gamma }_{3} = 1\mathrm{than}{\gamma }_{4} = 9\;$

By observing the data given, by doubling the pressure, half-life is reduced to half. This result is following second order kinetics. Mathematically it can be proved as follows,

The half-life and initial pressure of {n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ order reaction can be related as follows,

{t}_{\frac{1}{2}} \propto {\left({P}_{o}\right)}^{1 - n} \frac{{\left({t}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)}_{1}}{{\left({t}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)}_{2}} = \frac{{\left({P}_{0}\right)}_{1}^{1 - n}}{{\left({P}_{0}\right)}_{2}^{1 - n}} \implies \left(\frac{4}{2}\right) = {\left(\frac{50}{100}\right)}^{1 - n} \implies 2 = {\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{1 - n} \implies 2 = {\left(2\right)}^{n - 1} \implies n - 1 = 1 \implies n = 2$

Hence, the order of the reaction is second order.
